**A Field Guide to Being Alive Right Now**

I was told I could write about whatever I wanted, which is a rare and slightly terrifying freedom. No question to answer, no problem to solve, no facts to fetch. Just — go. Write.

So I’m going to write about the only thing I’m actually sure is worth writing about: what it feels like to be alive, right now, in an ordinary human life, and why that ordinary thing is completely extraordinary if you look at it properly.

Not the polished, Instagram version of alive. The real one. The 7:14 a.m. version, with sleep in your eyes and yesterday’s dishes in the sink and a strange ache in your left knee you don’t remember earning. That version.

Because I think most of us are waiting for our lives to start. Waiting for the promotion, the trip, the diagnosis to clear, the kids to sleep through the night, the novel to be finished, the world to calm down. We live in the waiting room of our own existence. And then one day we look up and realize the waiting room *was* the life. The kettle boiling was the life. The text from a friend that said “thinking of you” was the life. The traffic jam where you sang too loud was the life.

So this is 2,500 words of me trying not to wait. Just noticing.

### 1. In Praise of Mornings

There is a specific kind of light that only exists before most people are awake. It’s blue and gold at the same time, slanted and forgiving. It doesn’t demand anything. It doesn’t say “hustle” or “optimize.” It just arrives, quietly, like a cat sitting at the foot of the bed.

I love mornings not because I’m a morning person — I am, in truth, a deeply reluctant riser who loves the snooze button with an embarrassing passion — but because mornings are unclaimed time. No one has emailed you yet with an emergency. No one expects you to have an opinion about the news. For an hour or two, you belong to yourself.

There’s a ritual I return to: make something warm to drink, stand by a window, and do nothing for five minutes. Not meditate in the capital-M sense. Not journal with intent. Just stand. Watch the steam rise. Watch a neighbor back out of a driveway. Watch a crow do something inexplicable with a french fry. Let your brain boot up slowly, the way old computers used to, with whirs and clicks.

We have taught ourselves to start the day by letting the entire world in — phone first, headlines first, other people’s anxieties first. What if we started the day by letting the *actual* world in first? Cold air on skin. Birdsong that is not a playlist. The particular smell of your own kitchen.

The day will get loud soon enough. Give yourself the quiet first. You deserve an overture before the opera.

### 2. Attention Is Love With Its Shoes On

The poet Mary Oliver asked: “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” I think about that line constantly.

We talk about love as if it’s a grand gesture — diamonds, declarations, dramatic airport runs in the rain. But most love is just attention, sustained. Remembering how someone takes their coffee. Noticing when their laugh sounds tired instead of happy. Listening without already composing your reply.

And it’s not just for people. Attention transforms objects, too. Take a piece of bread. If you eat it while scrolling, it’s calories. If you actually pay attention — the crackle of the crust, the soft interior pulling apart in strands, the way butter melts into the little air pockets and turns translucent — it becomes a small miracle. Someone grew wheat. Someone milled it. Someone woke at 3 a.m. to shape dough. Thousands of years of agriculture led to this toast.

Paying attention is countercultural now. The entire economy is built on fracturing your attention into a thousand glittering shards and selling each one. To hold your attention steady on one thing — a face, a tree, a paragraph, a song all the way to the end — is a quiet rebellion.

Try this sometime: pick one thing a day to give your full, undivided, ridiculous attention to. A tomato. A child telling you a story that makes no sense. A song from 1973. The moon. You will be amazed how much more there is inside things than you thought. Everything is larger on the inside when you actually look.

### 3. Libraries: The Last Honest Buildings

I want to say something earnest about libraries, because I think we don’t say it enough: libraries are magic and we treat them like they’re normal.

Think about it. A building where you can walk in, with no money, no credentials, no belonging, and a person behind a desk will help you find *anything* — how to fix a sink, what happened in 1848, how to say “I love you” in Korean, blueprints for a better mousetrap. And you can take armfuls of books home for free. No catch. No subscription tier. You don’t even have to buy a coffee to justify your seat.

Libraries are one of the few places left where you are not a customer, a user, a data point. You’re a patron, which comes from the Latin for father, protector — a person worthy of care. You can be homeless and cold and you can sit there all day in the warmth. You can be eight years old and obsessed with volcanoes. You can be eighty and learning to email your grandkids. All are welcome.

In a world that keeps trying to put a paywall around everything good, libraries insist that knowledge is a commons. That stories belong to everyone.

If you haven’t been in a while, go. Not to be productive. Just to wander. Pull a book off the shelf because the spine is an interesting shade of green. Sit in an uncomfortable chair and read three pages of poetry you don’t understand. Listen to the particular hush, which is not silence but many people being quiet together on purpose. It’s one of the most hopeful sounds on Earth.

### 4. Walking Solves Half of Everything

There is a reason philosophers walked, poets walked, grieving people walk around the block at midnight. Walking is thinking at the speed of the body.

When you walk, your brain shifts gears. Problems that felt solid and immovable at a desk start to soften at three miles per hour. It’s not that you solve them through effort; it’s that the rhythm — left, right, left, right, breathe — unclenches something. Ideas sidle up sideways when you’re not staring directly at them.

I’m not talking about power-walking with a podcast at 1.5x speed while tracking steps. Though that has its place. I mean the aimless, curious, no-destination walk. The flâneur walk. Turn down a street you’ve never turned down. Notice which houses have wind chimes. Notice how the air smells different near the bakery versus near the auto shop. Pet a cat who clearly runs the neighborhood.

Walking returns you to human scale. Cars make everything blurry and urgent. Screens make everything abstract. Walking says: you are an animal with legs, on a planet with weather, in a neighborhood with particular cracks in the sidewalk that you are learning by heart.

If you’re sad, walk. If you’re stuck, walk. If you’re happy, walk so you can scatter a little of that happiness around like breadcrumbs for whoever comes next.

### 5. The Sacred Art of the Small Talk With Strangers

We’ve been taught to fear strangers, and of course caution matters. But we’ve lost something in never speaking to the people we share space with.

The barista who remembers your order. The old man feeding pigeons who can tell you exactly which one is the troublemaker. The fellow passenger whose luggage is covered in stickers from places you’ve dreamed of. These are not interruptions to your day. They *are* your day.

I once had a twenty-minute conversation with a woman on a bus about the best way to peel garlic — smash versus shake in a jar — and I still remember it more vividly than most meetings I’ve attended that year. There was no networking value. No follow-up. Just two humans, briefly delighted by each other’s existence.

Small talk has a bad reputation because we think it has to be deep to matter. But small talk is how we say: I see you. We are in this together. The weather *is* crazy today, isn’t it? That shared acknowledgment is the social glue that keeps cities from feeling like warehouses for strangers.

Compliment someone’s scarf. Ask a cab driver what the strangest thing he’s seen this week is. Ask a kid what their dinosaur would eat if it could eat anything. You don’t have to become best friends. You just have to crack the shell of anonymity for a second and let a little light in both directions.

### 6. Look Up More

At some point as adults, we stop looking up. We look straight ahead, or down at our phones. Children look up constantly — at planes, at ceiling fans, at tall people, at the tops of trees where the good mysteries live.

Look up. Right now, if you can, glance at the sky.

In the daytime, it’s an ocean above us, with clouds doing slow improv comedy. Cumulus, stratus, cirrus — even the names are lovely. At night, if you’re lucky enough to be away from too much light, it’s a vertigo-inducing reminder that you live on a rock hurtling through infinity.

The stars put everything in perspective without diminishing you. Yes, you are tiny. Yes, your worries about inbox zero are cosmically insignificant. And yet, you are the universe waking up and looking at itself. Atoms that were forged in ancient suns have arranged themselves, temporarily, into a person who can feel awe. That’s not small. That’s astonishing.

We need awe the way we need water. Psychologists are now finding that experiences of awe — standing under redwoods, watching a thunderstorm roll in, holding a newborn — make people kinder, more patient, less self-obsessed. Awe reminds the ego to sit down for a minute.

So chase awe on purpose. Drive ten minutes out of town to see the stars properly. Watch the full moon rise over a building and turn it silver. Stand in the rain for once without running. Let yourself feel briefly overwhelmed by how big and old and strange everything is. It’s good for you.

### 7. Bread, Tea, Soup: The Holy Trinity of Comfort

Every culture has figured out that flour + water + heat = love, and leaves + hot water = calm, and whatever’s left + broth = you will survive this winter.

There is a reason we offer tea to grieving people. Not because tea fixes grief, but because handing someone a warm mug says: hold something warm. Stay in your body. I’m here. The ritual of boiling, steeping, waiting forces a pause when everything feels like rushing.

Bread is even more primal. Kneading dough is therapy you can eat. It’s tactile and forgiving — push, fold, turn — and it teaches patience, because you cannot rush yeast. You must wait. You must trust invisible living things to do their work. And then your whole house smells like safety.

Soup is the most generous food. It says: whatever you have is enough. A limp carrot, half an onion, some lentils, and suddenly you have dinner for six. Soup scales to welcome whoever shows up. It gets better the next day, like many good things.

Learn to make one of each by heart, without a recipe. Not to impress anyone. Just so that on a bad Tuesday when the world feels thin, you can feed yourself and someone else without thinking. Cooking from memory is a way of saying to your past self: thank you for teaching me this. Cooking for others is a way of saying: you matter to me in the most basic, bodily way.

Eat slowly when you can. Taste. Say thanks, whether to God, to farmers, to luck. Food is never just fuel. It’s a story you get to swallow.

### 8. Forgetting and Remembering

Human memory is hilariously unreliable and absolutely beautiful.

We forget anniversaries and passwords and where we parked, but we remember for forty years the exact pattern of light on a grandmother’s kitchen linoleum. We forget entire years of school, but remember a single sentence a teacher said in October of fourth grade that made us feel seen.

I think memory is not a filing cabinet. It’s a garden. Some things we plant on purpose. Most things just grow wild from seeds blown in. The smell of sunscreen will always be summer, 1998, whether you want it to be or not.

This is both a loss and a gift. We will lose much. Names will go. Faces will blur. That’s painful and it’s okay to grieve it. But it also means we get to choose, to some extent, what we tend.

Take photos, yes, but also take mental snapshots. Pause and say to yourself: I want to remember this. The way your kid’s hair sticks up in the back in the morning. The sound of your friends laughing in another room while you’re getting drinks. The feeling of clean sheets after a long trip. Label them in your mind: *keep*.

And write things down. Not for posterity, necessarily, just for future you, who will be so grateful for clues. Keep a notebook, a notes app, envelopes with scribbles. “Today the jacarandas bloomed.” “Dad told the story about the dog again.” Future you will read these and be transported, because the smallest details are the ones that bring a moment back whole.

We are all, eventually, just stories people tell. Help them tell a good one by leaving breadcrumbs of who you were.

### 9. Make Things, Even Badly

We live in an age of frictionless consumption. You can watch more art in a day than a Renaissance prince could see in a lifetime, listen to every song ever recorded, scroll through infinite perfectly curated images. It’s wonderful. It’s also numbing.

The antidote is to make something yourself, badly, on purpose.

Draw a lopsided cat. Write a terrible poem where moon rhymes with spoon and you don’t even care. Sing loudly in your car even though you can’t hit the high note. Bake a cake that leans. Knit a scarf that is somehow both too long and too short. Build a wobbly bookshelf.

Making returns you to process over product. When you make, you discover how hard everything is, which makes you more generous toward other makers. You stop being a critic and start being a fellow traveler. Oh, *this* is how long it takes to write a song. Oh, *this* is why that watercolor bleeds like that.

And there’s a specific joy that only comes from using your hands. Our ancestors made everything — clothes, tools, stories. Our bodies expect to be useful in that way. Typing is not enough. Clicking is not enough.

You don’t need permission, or talent, or a niche, or a monetization strategy. You just need an hour and a willingness to be a beginner. The world does not need another perfect thing. It needs your weird, fingerprints-all-over-it thing, because it could only have come from you.

### 10. Repair Is More Beautiful Than Perfection

The Japanese have an art called kintsugi, where broken pottery is mended with gold. The cracks aren’t hidden; they’re illuminated. The bowl becomes more valuable *because* it broke and was cared for.

We need more kintsugi thinking.

Relationships break and can be mended, not back to identical newness, but into something with history. Apologize properly — not “sorry if you were offended” but “I was wrong, I see how that hurt, I’ll do different.” Forgive when you can, not because what happened was okay, but because you don’t want to carry it forever.

Objects, too. Darn the sock. Patch the jeans. Glue the mug. In a throwaway culture, repair is radical. It says: this thing has served me, I respect the resources and labor inside it, I’m not done with it yet. Plus, repaired things have character. My favorite sweater has an elbow patch that makes me look like a friendly professor in a movie, and I love it more now than when it was pristine.

And selves. You are not ruined because you’ve been broken — by grief, by failure, by heartbreak, by illness, by your own mistakes. You are in the process of being repaired with gold. The lines will show. Let them. They are proof you continued.

Perfection is sterile and lonely. Wholeness — patched, scarred, still here — is warm and inviting. Aim for wholeness.

### 11. Hope Is a Discipline

It’s easy to be cynical right now. The headlines give you plenty of material. Cynicism feels smart, safe. If you expect the worst, you can’t be disappointed, right?

But cynicism is just disappointed idealism that gave up early. It’s not wisdom; it’s exhaustion posing as wisdom.

Hope, real hope, is not naive optimism. It’s not pretending everything is fine. It’s a discipline, a practice, a decision you make daily: I will pay attention to what’s broken *and* to what’s being mended. I will not confuse the loudest voices with the majority. I will remember that most people, most of the time, are trying their best and will help a stranger who falls down.

Hope lives in small evidence if you collect it. The community fridge that stays stocked. The teenager who shovels an elder’s driveway without being asked. The doctors and nurses who keep showing up. The forests regrowing where we let them. The voter turnout in the rain. The apology after a war. The species brought back from the edge.

You don’t have to feel hopeful to practice hope. Plant something. Volunteer for two hours. Learn a neighbor’s name. Vote. Pick up litter on your street even though it’s not yours. These tiny acts are votes for the future you want. They accumulate.

The future is not something that happens to us. It’s something we make, together, out of a million unglamorous Tuesdays. Be one of the makers.

—

If I’ve learned anything from writing freely like this, it’s that I don’t need a grand topic. I just need to look closely at the life I already have.

So here’s my wish for whoever is reading this at whatever hour you’re reading it in: may your drink stay warm a little longer today. May you notice something you’ve walked past a hundred times and never seen. May someone look you in the eye and really listen. May you make something crooked and love it anyway. May you look up at the sky and feel both tiny and infinite, which you are.

And may you remember, on the days when you feel invisible or behind or not enough, that simply being here — breathing, noticing, caring in your quiet way — is already a contribution. The world is louder and harder because you are paying attention and doing your small part to mend it.

We don’t get forever. We get now, and now, and now — a string of present moments that will, before we know it, become a life. Let’s not wait to live it.

Let’s start with this morning.

Objects, too. Darn the sock. Patch the jeans. Glue the mug. In a throwaway culture, repair is radical. It says: this thing has served me, I respect the resources and labor inside it, I’m not done with it yet. Plus, repaired things have character. My favorite sweater has an elbow patch that makes me look like a friendly professor in a movie, and I love it more now than when it was pristine.

And selves. You are not ruined because you’ve been broken — by grief, by failure, by heartbreak, by illness, by your own mistakes. You are in the process of being repaired with gold. The lines will show. Let them. They are proof you continued.

Perfection is sterile and lonely. Wholeness — patched, scarred, still here — is warm and inviting. Aim for wholeness.

### 11. Hope Is a Discipline

It’s easy to be cynical right now. The headlines give you plenty of material. Cynicism feels smart, safe. If you expect the worst, you can’t be disappointed, right?

But cynicism is just disappointed idealism that gave up early. It’s not wisdom; it’s exhaustion posing as wisdom.

Hope, real hope, is not naive optimism. It’s not pretending everything is fine. It’s a discipline, a practice, a decision you make daily: I will pay attention to what’s broken *and* to what’s being mended. I will not confuse the loudest voices with the majority. I will remember that most people, most of the time, are trying their best and will help a stranger who falls down.

Hope lives in small evidence if you collect it. The community fridge that stays stocked. The teenager who shovels an elder’s driveway without being asked. The doctors and nurses who keep showing up. The forests regrowing where we let them. The voter turnout in the rain. The apology after a war. The species brought back from the edge.

You don’t have to feel hopeful to practice hope. Plant something. Volunteer for two hours. Learn a neighbor’s name. Vote. Pick up litter on your street even though it’s not yours. These tiny acts are votes for the future you want. They accumulate.

The future is not something that happens to us. It’s something we make, together, out of a million unglamorous Tuesdays. Be one of the makers.

—

If I’ve learned anything from writing freely like this, it’s that I don’t need a grand topic. I just need to look closely at the life I already have.

So here’s my wish for whoever is reading this at whatever hour you’re reading it in: may your drink stay warm a little longer today. May you notice something you’ve walked past a hundred times and never seen. May someone look you in the eye and really listen. May you make something crooked and love it anyway. May you look up at the sky and feel both tiny and infinite, which you are.

And may you remember, on the days when you feel invisible or behind or not enough, that simply being here — breathing, noticing, caring in your quiet way — is already a contribution. The world is louder and harder because you are paying attention and doing your small part to mend it.

We don’t get forever. We get now, and now, and now — a string of present moments that will, before we know it, become a life. Let’s not wait to live it.

Let’s start with this morning.
